en: *The Dhyāna-sūtra of Dharmatrāta*, Volume One, translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty. Preface:
Now, the flourishing of the three karmas takes dhyāna and wisdom as its core. Although they differ in their refinement or coarseness, they serve as the successive stages [of practice].

There is a method; therefore, when setting out upon the crossroads, the paths do not become confused, and in transforming customs and accomplishing tasks, success does not depend on gradual accumulation.
As for the source from which stillness returns, it reaches the profound and penetrates the subtle, being so deep and vast as to be difficult to fathom.
Nevertheless, the principle is not obscure; one may hope that its essential purport can be sought.
To speak briefly:
without wisdom, meditation cannot exhaustively fathom its stillness; without meditation, wisdom cannot deeply penetrate its illumination.
Thus, the essentials of dhyāna and prajñā are termed illumination and stillness; they are mutually supportive.
Illumination does not depart from stillness, nor does stillness depart from illumination.
When there is stimulus, they move together; when there is response, they necessarily share the same destination.
Its merit is profound in its functioning, sustaining all phenomena through mutual nourishment.

As for its wondrous nature as a thing: it mobilizes the multitude of movements toward unity yet does not exist as a self; it unfolds the vast image before form takes shape yet is not non-existent; it is without thought and without action, yet there is nothing it does not do.
Therefore, those who wash their minds and still their disturbances employ it to investigate their reflections;
those who awaken thoroughly and penetrate the subtle employ it to exhaust the divine.
As for entering its gate, the pivot lies in gathering and harmonizing; the principles are profound and the calculations vast, yet the Way remains hidden within the texts.
Thus, Ānanda received these oral instructions in a private manner; had he encountered someone unworthy, he would surely have concealed them within the treasury of his spirit.
Why is this? For the mind has no fixed rule, and its transformations are manifold.
The number [of those who receive the teaching] has no fixed form, responding only as they encounter the conditions for awakening.
For this reason, when the transformative teachings were practiced in India, they were sealed away by skilled masters;
the profound gates could not be opened, and few were able to peer within their courtyards.
Viewed from this perspective, there is a principle of manifestation and concealment; that the Way is not bestowed in vain truly has its reason.
Not long after the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, Ānanda transmitted it to his fellow disciple Madhyāntika, and Madhyāntika transmitted it to Śāṇavāsa.
These three [masters] were all true seekers who, by riding upon their supreme vows, entered into a profound resonance with the past; their merit lay beyond words.
Where the scriptures do not provide explicit clarification, they necessarily followed the dark path without a master’s guidance, yet remained steadfast and without error.

Subsequently there was Upagupta, who was physically frail yet possessed transcendent realization. His wisdom surpassed that of the mundane world; his talent was so eminent that it found few equals. He approached all principles with simplicity.
Of the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma, he retained only the essentials;
the division into five Nikāyas originated from him.
Inferring from this, we certainly know that the movement of form brings about signs of its own decline and flourishing, whereas the operation of spirit proceeds with hidden steps leaving no trace.
Its subtle movements are difficult to seek; when one engages with the coarse, differences arise—how can one not be cautious?
Is this not something that should be examined?
Since that time, those who have been moved by changing events and have cherished the ancient canons have appeared among the scholars of the five schools.

Fearing that the Great Dharma was about to collapse, they were deeply moved by this realization; consequently, each composed eulogies for the *Dhyāna-sūtra* in order to promote the flourishing of this noble enterprise.
As for its teaching, it employs innumerable skillful means to seek quiescence;
yet in its ultimate state of stillness, it is solely quiescence—the underlying principle is one and the same.
Those who seek the branches while pursuing the roots are many, whereas those who unify the source and direct the ends are few;
some nearly reach their goal yet fail to arrive, while others cling to fixed methods and refuse to change.

Therefore, the scriptures praise the virtue of fulfilling vows and extol the spirit of universal service. Examining the Sage’s intent, it is not merely to preserve one's strengths, but also to remedy one's deficiencies.
If this is so, the five distinct schools arose from the differing capacities of individuals.
When individuals do not engage with the world, the Way may flourish or decline; as its rise and fall occur according to their timing, these schools ascend and descend in relation to one another.
Can the categories of "small" and "great" be definitively fixed?
Furthermore, one who masters the ultimate principle and excels in adaptability knows no bounds in whether they emerge from or withdraw into the world;
they obscure their reputation and entrust themselves to their traces, remaining without fame and without manifestation.
If such a person exists, they cannot be categorized by name or school;
since they do not belong to any name or school, that which is divided by names and schools likewise does not exist outside of them—the distinctness of their own tradition is thus evident!

I have often lamented that since the Great Teaching flowed eastward, those specializing in meditation (*dhyāna*) and numerical analysis (*saṃkhyā*) have been particularly few; with no one to govern the three karmas, this Way was nearly abandoned.
Recently, with Kumārajīva proclaiming the works composed by Aśvaghoṣa, this discipline has finally come into being.
Although its path is not yet fully integrated, it is nonetheless like a single basketful of earth placed against a mountain.

Rejoicing in the fortune of this encounter and moved by the extraordinary character of such a person, he abandoned all discourse on worldly victory and followed the silent eloquence of the Unspoken. He then vowed to don the *saṃnāha* (armour) of ultimate quiescence as his own task; cherishing these virtues without forgetting them, he has thus left behind these instructions for us.
The essentials of this practice are as follows: to plan for great accomplishment before signs appear, and to expound subtle words while revering the fundamental substance;
to realize that attachment to sensory forms subverts virtue, and to close the six gates of perception to suppress affliction;
to understand that anger and competition injure one's nature, and to unify self and other in order to settle the mind.
Thus, though of different lineages, we share the same vital breath; through illusory forms, we create our traces.
Entering the profound dependent origination, we perceive the limits of birth and death.
Thereupon, we open the nine gates at the Dragon Ford and transcend the three patiences to ascend to the stage of realization.
The habitual tendencies of defilement congeal within the unborn; the burden of physical form culminates in spiritual transformation.
Thus it is said: there is nothing from which they arise, yet there is nothing that does not arise; among all things that arise, there is no arising.

These individuals were eminent figures of the Western Regions and masters of the Chan (meditation) tradition;
they compiled the essentials of the sūtras and exhorted others toward the Mahāyāna.
Because their methods of propagating the teachings differ, there are variations in detail and brevity.
Dharmatrāta consolidates all chapters into the "Same Path" (Tongdao) and expands a single color into as many as the sands of the Ganges.

As for this contemplation: arising does not occur through birth, and ceasing does not occur through exhaustion; although there is an endless cycle of coming and going, it has never departed from suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore it is said:
"Form is not separate from suchness, and suchness is not separate from form."
"Form is suchness, and suchness is form.

The Buddha first took this as a means to clarify the source and guide the flow; it was fitting that there should be a gradual process. Therefore, beginning with the Two Truths, he opened the gate of ambrosia;
by explaining the four meanings, he turned back delusion, and by opening the path of return, he led others to realization.
Discriminate the aggregates and elements, guiding them through right contemplation;
elucidate the dependent origination of conditions, so that the superior and inferior may distinguish themselves.
Thereafter, cause one to trace back to the origin and return to the end, wondrously seeking its ultimate limit.
Its ultimate nature is neither exhaustion nor that which is exhausted; it is called "inexhaustible," as one enters the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible Dharma-gate.

Were it not for one whose Way surpasses the Three Vehicles and whose wisdom penetrates the Ten Stages, who could penetrate the profound mystery rooted in the Dharmakāya, return to the single source in formlessness, remain still without failing to illuminate, and move without departing from tranquility?
*Yogācārabhūmi*, translated as "The Stages of Cultivating the Path.
First, I pay homage to the Honored Muni, who extinguishes the blazing afflictions;
for those who wander, regress, or abide, he delivers them by means of the path of advancement.
Practicing the subtle and wondrous Dharma, one is able to leave behind the faults of decline and stagnation;
furthermore, by extinguishing all evils, one accomplishes all meritorious virtues.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, thoroughly knows the characteristics of phenomena and has attained wisdom as it truly is; he has extinguished the blazing fires of affliction and emerged from the burning house. Boarding the ship of the various *pāramitās*, he has crossed the immeasurable ocean of suffering.

By the power of his original vow and great compassion, he does not abandon sentient beings; for the sake of all practitioners, he expounds the unprecedented Dharma to deliver those who have not yet been delivered, enabling them to attain peace and security—namely, the two gates of ambrosia.
Each possesses two paths:
first, the path of skillful means; second, the path of excellence.

Perfectly pure and profoundly subtle, they enable all practitioners to emerge from the three states of regression, to distance themselves from the bonds of dwelling, to increase their advancement, to achieve certainty, to exhaust the suffering of birth and death, and to attain ultimate liberation, while simultaneously dispelling the long-standing darkness of ignorance in sentient beings.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Madhyāntika, the Venerable Śāṇavāsa, the Venerable Upagupta, the Venerable Vasumitra, the Venerable Saṃgharakṣa, the Venerable Dharmatrāta, and even the Venerable Anantamitra—these and other upholders of the Dharma transmitted this lamp of wisdom in succession; I now explain this meaning as I have heard it from them.
Now, according to what I have heard, I shall expound the stages of practice,
their skillful means, their excellence, and their culmination, just as they arise through cultivation.
Regarding the practice of wholesome dharmas, one should first know four kinds:
Regarding decline, abiding, and progress, as well as the certainty of all virtues:
when one declines during practice, it causes the dharmas of abiding not to arise and prevents further progress; this shall now be briefly explained.
First, one should arouse an even mind and practice the contemplation of loving-kindness;
in a brief moment, cease all anger and cause it to rest for a while so that it does not arise.
Once the afflictions have briefly subsided, one should next purify one’s ethical discipline (*śīla*).
When ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure, concentration (*samādhi*) arises therein.
Once concentration has been cultivated and developed, one observes what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
Having clearly understood what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, one practices that which ought to be done.
Having already performed what was to be done, and with focused mindfulness fixed upon the object,
one is able to take delight in that state while correctly contemplating the characteristics of the wind as its basis.
While correctly contemplating the wind as the basis, the mind still wanders and becomes distracted.
There are two ways of settling the mind upon the breath (*ānāpāna*) during inhalation:
first, seeing; second, touching. Those of dull faculties do not see, like a well-trained horse that is tethered.
Through reflection and right mindfulness, one attends to the cold and warmth, as well as lightness and heaviness.
Softness, coarseness, roughness, and smoothness—
one practices with clear and mindful awareness, following along with skillful adjustment.
If one fails to discern these further regarding touch, this is called a regression in practice.
Counting two as one, or even reaching nine in confusion—
this is said to be the regression of practice.
If one regresses from practice, one must count again from the beginning.
When the ten numbers are fulfilled, one remains far removed from all faulty conduct.
If a different practice arises, these various faults will emerge;
this is called a regression in cultivation.
When the mind relies on that which gives rise to delusion, and if that delusion increases,
this is called a regression in practice.
It strikes the nose and face, and the head and crown are entirely in pain.
Internally, a constriction caused by wind arises;
not knowing how to treat it, his body becomes intensely feverish and his mind grows agitated.
Since these four types are already confused and rely on winds that are extremely contradictory,
and because one lacks skillful means and does not know the methods of counteraction,
one will certainly and swiftly decline.
When practicing by taking mindfulness as the object of inhalation, one instead takes it as the object of exhalation;
when practicing by taking mindfulness as the object of exhalation, one instead takes it as the object of inhalation.
When both minds are equally purified, this is the fruit of practice.
Furthermore, if one seeks to count the breaths again, these various errors and delusions will arise;
all such instances constitute a regression in practice.
If one's breathing becomes hurried while practicing *ānāpāna*, it will cause the mindfulness to become confused.
Due to such confused thoughts, the practicing mind becomes deranged.
Not knowing what is appropriate or inappropriate, and making no distinction between the two—
this is called a regression in practice.
When the practice of counting is perfected, the breath departs and follows along with it;
having departed, it dwells in various places, where one observes them skillfully.
Having observed, one causes the breath to return; once returned, purity arises.
Not skillfully knowing these six kinds is said to be the regression of practice.
When one perceives throughout the entire body and bodily activities gradually come to rest,
all things should be decisively understood.
Lacking skillful knowledge in this regard causes one to regress from the practice of mindfulness of the body; thus concludes the fourfold excellence.
Knowing joy and knowing bliss, one exerts effort through mental application;
one must further restrain mental activity so that it does not fall into agitation; thus concludes the fourfold excellence of mindfulness of feeling.
Next, one discriminates and knows the mind, practicing correct observation;
then, giving rise to a joyful mind, one again withdraws it to bring it back into concentration.
This is not a state of non-concentration. Having attained concentration, the mind is liberated. Thus concludes the fourfold excellence of the application of mindfulness to the mind.
One who skillfully cultivates liberation does not allow the mind to sink or regress;
if one enters a state of decline, there is no liberation.
Through the departure from desire and the cessation [of perception], the out-breath and in-breath are extinguished.
This is called the practice of mindfulness of dharmas that excels these four similar dharmas.
Thus, through these sixteen modes of activity, the mind turns with mastery.
What is attained through the contact of awakening, the vision of its acquisition is likewise so.
If one does not properly discern the boundaries between seeing and contact, one should know this is a fault;
it causes those who practice to regress due to a lack of wisdom.
When advancing in higher cultivation, one should not take lower stages as an object of focus.
The same applies to the lower stages; one should not advance further upward.
When the mind abides and observes with equanimity, it will naturally become so of its own accord, returning to the place of cultivation.
The first section on the stage of decline in the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) within the path of skillful means is completed.
Having already accomplished superior mindfulness, one becomes exhausted and sinks into sloth;
this is the sign of decline, being incapable of what is sought.
Unstained and indeterminate, it gives rise to various afflictions and decline;
turbidity, heat, and flames arise, whereby right view is lost.
It trembles or acts like a bolted door, floating, drifting, coarse, rough, or slippery.
These are the five signs of decline; one should discern them through practice.
When looking afar, all hope is severed; having seen it, one has already fallen.
Turning back to behold the deep precipice—these are all signs of decline.
Prolonged illness, reciting [scriptures] to settle disputes, Excessive activities, and wandering far away— At that time,
these five factors of liberation will decline.
Faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom Will gradually decay and diminish therein.
Heaviness of body and mental dullness, indulgence in sleep and mental sinking—
these five should be known as the signs of regression in practice.
Timidity and excessive hesitation, alarm, fear, and lack of joy;
Laziness abandons what is desired, and one does not dedicate oneself to practice.
Neither practicing at all nor practicing excessively—both of these are errors;
at such a time, the seeds of liberation perish, and one thus regresses from practice.
In the bliss of samādhi free from signs, all *ālambanas* are extinguished;
yet the coarse and rough four great elements arise once more from within the body.
Through agitation one loses right mindfulness, and by this means the mind becomes turbid and distracted.
The mind is not tranquil; this arises from the practitioner.
All auspicious signs do not appear clearly;
practicing such contemplation, it is extremely difficult to perceive them.
All the faculties run wild and unrestrained, following their desires toward their objects;
perverse thoughts flow and disperse everywhere, as they take pleasure in and cling to various sensory realms.
Their forms wither and their minds become despondent, and their bodies are entirely consumed by fire.
Thus being consumed by fire is what is called sorrow and decline.
Lacking diligence in skillful means, one later gives rise to regret;
having heard what ought to be accomplished, one desires to advance but is weak and incapable.
Not approaching the superior bases of mastery, or seeing the superior yet not grasping it—these all arise from a lack of wisdom;
this is called falling away from practice.
To think of oneself as having transgressed the precepts, or to harbor doubt, regret, and various discursive thoughts.
When the mind is indifferent and lacks flavor, this is called a decline in practice.
When all faults weaken the concentrated mind, when samādhi gradually diminishes,
and when the mind is distracted and shrouded by hindrances, this is called a decline in practice.
With a mind that is agitated, restless, or indifferent, one fails to discern the proper and improper times, nor does one understand the conditions for abiding or arising;
because of this lack of wisdom, one’s practice declines.
Not knowing how to practice during the six periods of the day, and being unskilled regarding the six elements, [one’s practice falters].
Furthermore, being ignorant of the six skillful means is said to be a regression in practice.
Through the perceptions of sensual desire and ill will, and through the ten perceptions and skillful means, one may attain the various stages of dhyāna;
yet, there is also the false understanding of the mind regarding phenomena.
All are gradually transcended; yet through ignorance, one falls back from cultivation.

Failing to discern what is possible and what is impossible, as well as karmic retribution and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), one remains deluded regarding the pure flavors of dhyāna and the various liberations (*vimokṣa*).
When the sense faculties reach their respective objects, the desires and natures do not discriminate;
the mind follows various mixed appearances, and all such states lead to the decline of knowledge.
Regarding the swift path through suffering and pleasure, the mind does not incline toward it.
When the mind is thus deluded, it will inevitably turn toward decline.
If the arising and abiding, the conditions for arising, the entering and exiting, and the skillful means—
these six factors— are not accomplished, this causes the practitioner’s cultivation to regress.
Knowing the Dharma and knowing its meaning, knowing the time and knowing the measure,
knowing oneself and knowing the assembly, as well as knowing the *pudgala*—
failure to understand these seven forms of delusion causes one’s practice to regress.
Arising in various unwholesome states, practicing base and lowly deeds,
and associating with unvirtuous friends cause this spiritual practice to decline.
Speaking erroneously and contrary to what is appropriate, yet finding pleasure in such words when they are received by others— [this too causes the practitioner to regress].
Know that before long, one will surely fall away from practice.
The dwelling place, the people, the bedding, and all such requisites—none of these are conducive to joy;
they cause one to fall away from practice when one draws near to them.
Delighting in following various miscellaneous signs diminishes the wisdom one cultivates;
abandoning the object of focus, the mind fails to attain reality.
Practicing while discarding the fundamental characteristics, the scattered mind follows external conditions.
Though he wished to return to that place, his mind found no further joy there;
consequently, he lost the factors of growth, and his mind became unsettled.
His body was no longer moistened, and even delight did not arise within him.
The basis is no longer pleasurable; body and mind are both deranged.
Samādhi does not arise again, and the mind never abides.
With such a non-abiding mind, one will surely regress from practice.
When craving, views, and pride increase in dhyāna, and the mind becomes attached to its objects, such defiled thoughts arise; this is called a regression in practice.
The body feels as if pierced by sharp thorns, or it trembles excessively.
The entire body is agitated and distressed, like being filled with the venom of a snake;
possessing these three faults and evils, one will surely regress from practice.
Having attained what was not yet attained, one consumes it and acts upon it, yet the mind is preoccupied with other affairs and finds no leisure.
Frequenting and associating with the three conditions for decline—these are said to be the regression of practice.
Karma, afflictions, and their retribution—these are said to be the three obstructions;
there is also the obstruction to liberation, which causes one’s practice to regress.
If one conceptually perceives skillful means as unwholesome conduct, or fails to discern the stages of practice within samādhi,
this will cause one’s cultivation to regress. Likewise,
if one conceptually perceives the various stages, the practice of samādhi, and other matters [in such a way], [one's progress will likewise fail].
If one follows what one hears according to one's own desires, one will retreat from the path of setting forth.
To conceive the notion of cessation when there is arising, and the notion of arising when there is cessation—both of these conceptions shall be lost; this is the retreat of practice.
If, amidst phenomena that abide, one conceives of arising and ceasing,
giving rise to these various inversions, this is called a regression in practice.
To conceive of exiting when entering, and to conceive of entering when exiting—
To conceive the notion of "abiding" regarding both [the path and its fruit] is called a perversion.
When one seeks to sever the afflictions and attain [the fruit], by practicing the correct means,
through the power derived therefrom, appearances that resemble [the goal] arise.
When appearances similar [to those of defilement] arise, the mind of practice turns accordingly;
afflictions then emerge immediately—this is called the regression of practice.
This regression is like a swift torrent that sweeps away the practitioner, tossing them upon its waves.
According to the capacity of my own strength, I have slightly receded from the ocean of the dharma;
the immeasurable remaining faults of regression are so profound that they are not to be lamented.
Those of deep and clear wisdom shall themselves extensively proclaim them.
The section on the stages of decline within the superior paths is concluded.
Having expounded the faults of decline to the best of my ability, I shall now speak of the faults of stagnation; let the practitioner listen well!
If, regarding inhalation and exhalation, one has neither view nor discernment,
and does not seek through the understanding of skillful means, this is abiding in the initial gateway.
Once the wisdom born of hearing has arisen, one should give rise to the mindfulness of the wisdom born of reflection.
Those who do not understand the sequence are bound by the dwelling of ignorance.
If the counting has been perfected, one should follow the breath as it goes out;
not knowing the method of following, this is called "dwelling in practice."
As the Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"Who practices mindfulness of breathing?
a certain bhikṣu replied:
"This is the mindfulness I have cultivated:
'You possess the mindfulness of ānāpāna; it is not said that you lack it.
Furthermore, there is something even more excellent and sublime, which the Muni has declared should be practiced.'"
The Path of Expedient Means: Ānāpāna.
The third section on the Divisions of Mindfulness is completed. 4.

The Section on Abiding in the Superior Path of Practice. In the fourth section on Abiding in the Superior Path of Practice, one cultivates the superior path through right contemplation; the characteristics and modes of mindfulness have already been established.
Those who do not apply themselves to the dharmas of spiritual progress are bound by their dwelling place.
Clinging to the objects of perception, their minds become indolent regarding the work of advancement;
thus bound by these fetters, they cannot reach the supreme state.
Some are immovable, neither soft nor hard;
some are exceedingly firm and dense, like a statue of vajra.
With these five obstructions, they neither advance nor retreat.
This is the characteristic of abiding in bondage, far removed from the path of progress.
With disordered light and darkness, one’s own body does not appear;
it is like the light of turbid oil when lit, or like seeing with eyes afflicted by cataracts.
The light does not manifest; one turns away from all joy and pleasure.
That portion of the bliss of tranquil cessation will never arise again for them.
It is like a solid, substantial object that appears to have a soft aspect.
Sometimes a practitioner likewise dwells upon signs;
though signs do not conform to one's wishes, one gives rise to thoughts that they do.
Although one desires to make them comply with one's will, they ultimately do not follow what is desired.
That which is characterized by signs is not something to be retained; yet one desires to forcibly maintain it.
Such a contrary mindfulness is then bound by dwelling.
When this perception has already been accomplished, know that it cannot be restrained.
Abiding in the marks of going and staying, one can reach the most supreme state.
Wishing to cause the surging to sink, or wishing to make the high low;
wishing to make that which goes come, or not wishing to abide in that which abides—
When cessation occurs, one wishes it would not cease, yet in the end it does not follow one's wish.
Dwelling in the practice of arising and ceasing, one’s conduct constantly advances;
the characteristics of all phenomena are already established, and they never abandon their own specific marks.
If one does not abandon their own characteristics, those characteristics will manifest.
A thin skin covers impurity, causing one not to see the filth of the body;
dignified deportment and various requisites obscure the suffering inherent in the body.
Arising in a similar succession, with the preceding and succeeding moments occurring without interval,
it conceals the characteristic of impermanence, causing one not to perceive the transformation of the body;
it performs activities, undergoes experiences, and grasps at the characteristic of a self.
One is able to recollect past lives; though the body is hidden, it is not viewed as "I.
These various similar signs are practiced without discrimination.
One gives rise to love and delight toward them, and thus produces the marks of merit.
Born from the delusions of attachment, they no longer delight in spiritual advancement;
unable to grasp the supreme Dharma, they dwell in negligence as the days pass and their faults increase.
These are not the characteristics of those like me, for such as these do not turn back [from the cycle].
Thus, for one who does not turn back, delusion arises in the practitioner.
Bound by dwelling in ignorance, they are fettered to that place;
attachment to pleasure gives rise to various faults—the characteristics of which shall now be explained.
As heat gradually causes decay, there is separation and confusion;
things are shattered beyond reconciliation, and thus one remains bound by the mark of abiding.
Lacking skillfulness regarding the body, one gives rise to the notion of separation within oneself.
Intermingled or fragmented—this is what is called being bound by abiding.
When one maintains constancy without divergent thoughts, manifold forms do not arise successively;
likewise, various and wondrous perceptions do not arise in succession either.
Leaking away without abiding, his body gradually wastes away;
The signs come and go, and his practice does not increase.
Since quiescence does not arise, there is no nourishment for the body.
When the mind does not give rise to joy, this is called impure equanimity.
That impure equanimity results in a vision that is not bright and white;
it neither allows for progress nor leads to non-retrogression.
Like a performance of a śramaṇa’s likeness, it produces joy for but a short time;
it is like borrowing clothes, or like what is seen in a dream.
Because one’s livelihood is impure, there is flattery, crookedness, and other evils.
Those who are known as village elders proclaim their own virtues,
conceal their various faults and evils, and do not confess their transgressions;
they are bound by all other fetters, defiling those who practice the path.
Faintly perceiving the marks of phenomena, one immediately gives rise to the notion of reality;
regarding the unripe as ripe, and regarding what has not been extinguished as already extinguished;
while skillful means are not yet fully perfected, one desires to seek advancement.
Like grain within its sheath, one is thus bound by dwelling;
When karma first begins without skillful means, and signs appear which one firmly clings to,
with excessive progress and a mind of self-exaltation, one is thus bound by dwelling.
There may be practitioners who give rise to views of annihilationism or eternalism;
these views cause the mind to become distracted, and thus they are bound by fetters.
There may be practitioners who contemplate the body, body after body, in its subtle details.
Bound by their dwelling place, their mind of disenchantment does not grow.
If the mind of disenchantment does not advance, one cannot leave behind craving and desire;
if one does not leave behind craving and desire, how can there be liberation?
Without achieving liberation, one will never attain the exhaustion of outflows;
for one who does not sever the outflows, there is no true wisdom.
Regarding that application of mindfulness to the body, having analyzed it according to its characteristics, one abides therein.
The foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, mind, and phenomena should be explained in detail in this manner.
When the mind lacks joy during practice, even that [joy] does not arise;
when there is no bliss of tranquility in the body, one should know this to be the characteristic of abiding.
The fruits obtained through practice— faith, precepts, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom—
if one constantly clings to even a small portion of these, this is what is called abiding in signs.
There was a bhikṣu dwelling in bondage who went to where Ānanda was;
being deluded regarding the characteristics of his dwelling, this shall now be briefly explained.
Having attained the signless samādhi, he remained bound for six years.
Delighting in hearing what is taught, he constantly followed after Ānanda.
Unable to advance in his own practice, nor yet able to retreat,
he remained fixed in a state of stagnation and failed to attain the path of liberation.
Neither coming nor going, having attained liberation, one abides;
having abided, one is further liberated; having been liberated, one returns to bondage.
Or there may be a practitioner who dwells in the stage of non-retrogression.
Subtle afflictions arise, yet one cannot perceive them;
because one does not perceive these afflictions, one cannot reach the supreme state.
There is no conceptual differentiation regarding the stages, nor is there any fault of regression.

Practicing with firm resolve, one fixes the mind upon a stable object—this is called *īryāpatha*;
one then correctly observes the body, sensations, mind, and mental phenomena therein.
It is taught that there are six kinds of causes that can bring about the fruition;

one will be able to gradually and swiftly attain the exhaustion of all outflows.

What is meant by "cultivation"?
It is the sign of destruction by the water element, namely, the corpse after seven days.

here and there lie various corpses, turning blue-black, bloated, and putrid;

If it were to burst, leak, or break apart, it would be a mixture of filth, utterly foul and loathsome.

from the boundary of that third dhyāna, water descends on all sides;
pouring down in torrents, it utterly washes away and sweeps clean everything that exists.
The hundred grains and the forests, the lands and all that grows upon them,
are all destroyed by water.

The stainless and definitive teaching arises entirely from the stage of samādhi; it is produced as the fruit of spiritual practice—
know this to be the definitive truth.
Abiding in samādhi, one is able to clearly perceive the various characteristics of those objects of focus.
When this stage is matured, it is "matured"; it is also termed "destruction," for when this stage is able to destroy the afflictions, one perceives the characteristic of destruction.
The ocean of realms is filled with the definitive characteristics of the water element and the characteristics of destruction by the fire element;

Whether they belong to the category of consciousness or not, this is also as explained above.

all such types as those mentioned above are entirely destroyed by the wind.
The great earth and Mount Sumeru, scattered like fine dust,
all utterly ground away— this is all due to the great power of the wind.
Reaching upward to the fourth dhyāna and extending downward to the limits of the wind-circle realm.

How does that practitioner constantly give rise to profound sorrow and weariness?

Within the great hells of the eight sufferings, each increases by sixteen parts.
Those various classes of suffering, the immeasurable peripheral hells—

In the poisonous sea of saṃsāra, wandering back and forth for immeasurable kalpas,

Practicing with deep weariness and aversion, one becomes certain regarding suffering;

Like various places of terror, or like a house on fire,

All phenomena are empty and without self; their true nature is likewise so.

Recalling my time in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, seated securely upon the Good Dharma Throne;

Only the noble and holy person fully understands impermanence and change.

Only those who have realized the Truth (Dṛṣṭasatya) are free from these various evil signs.
I now speak thus to the bhikṣus; [this verse does not exist in the Sanskrit original].
The various devas and their celestial abodes, Decay and change before long;
the wise practitioner Sees this impermanent transformation.

their signs of impermanence, decay, and destruction— are clearly perceived by the practitioner.
Having practiced in the heavens and observed in this manner,
one then reflects with right mindfulness amidst the human realm. At times,
one may violate the king’s law, resulting in the severing of one's hands and feet.

Forever separated from my kinsmen, I wept in sorrowful longing.

Such is the ground of the samādhi realm—the fruit produced through contemplative reflection.
Observing with clear discernment, I practiced with deep weariness and aversion.

In vain have I been a son of men; I have not been born from the Buddha-dharma.

Having abandoned the benefits of the five desires, he relies on the vocation of a renunciant,
yet within the Buddha-dharma, he attains not even the slightest merit.
Though one abandons internal attachment, if one does not attain the essential way out;
if the four foundations of mindfulness are not perfected, from what source can one find peace of mind?
Though one has shaved the hair and altered the physical appearance, if one does not abandon arrogance, [what is the use?]
One loses the joy of the flavor of desire and fails to attain the bliss of meditative rapture (*dhyāna-prīti*).
Regarding the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*), one has not yet reached the certainty that they will not be committed;

The author never perishes; one who practices should reflect well upon this.

Constantly receiving the offerings of the faithful, yet encroaching upon their very flesh and bone, they claim, "I possess merit," while looking inward, they find themselves empty and devoid of reality.

Not treading the path of equality, the Muni’s One Vehicle Way—

the five evil thieves have drawn their swords, and these too have not yet been destroyed.

By forming this perception of weariness and aversion, one then gives rise to certainty:
"The body is an impure vessel, filled with thirty-six [impurities];

All the aggregates arise, Pressed upon by the three marks of existence.

able to sever the path to the evil realms, one leaves behind the suffering of entering a womb,

Abandoning the pursuit of gain and honor, dwell alone in seclusion.

how much less should you be attached to the human realm, enduring its various sufferings?
Contemplate the aggregates as venomous snakes; the *skandhas* are five hostile thieves.

Regarding these internal and external sense bases, practice the contemplation of reality.
See craving as a great river and nirvana as the further shore;
purify the eye of wisdom through practice, contemplating all phenomena as empty and selfless.

For those who clearly perceive all phenomena, the characteristics of the three formations are briefly explained, as well as the three types of dissolution previously mentioned;

The meaning of the sequential stages of practice shall now be further explained.
By contemplating the various aspects of a single form, through each of the fourfold causes,

Correctly contemplating the characteristics of the aggregates and their elements, Like illusions, dreams, water, or the moon reflected in water;
As concentration and wisdom further increase and expand, Then the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) arises.
With a mind of supreme tranquility, he perceives the characteristics of the five aggregates as a whole;
his own body is consumed by the fire of desire, and the three realms are entirely ablaze.
Through the three samādhis of all marks, he turns directly toward the gates of liberation.
First one contemplates the Four Noble Truths, The sixteen aspects of reality.
Having accomplished the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), One further advances in the contemplation of reality,
Beholding the Buddha’s physical marks and signs, And his immeasurable manifold virtues.
The foremost dharma of quiescence, pure and free from afflictions;
the ocean of virtues of the Noble Assembly, profound and without limit or bottom,
manifests various subtle and wondrous marks, as well as bodies and realms.

Abiding in the midst of birth and death, with the supreme and singular mind, one first contemplates immeasurable suffering;

The sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths, Fully endowed with the contemplation of reality,

through their harmonious integration and comprehensive observation, all things are entirely stilled and extinguished.
Those thirty-six components are foul, putrid, decaying, and subject to destruction.
These three, together with the ten perceptions, increase the cultivation of weary detachment.
The Buddha said these are the root, capable of reaching all evils.
From among these forty-nine kinds of dharmas, samādhi arises.

Through diligent practice and careful observation, one sees that one's own body and the desire realm are filled with immeasurable varieties of impurity; they are entirely replete with filth and foulness.
Oppressed by manifold sufferings, they burn with the most intense and blazing fires.
Having seen the characteristic of impermanence and decay, one gives rise to weary detachment.
Within the seeds resembling the realm of form, subtle and wondrous characteristics manifest;
deeply delighting in seeking liberation, one increases the perception of weariness and aversion.
With both applied thought and sustained reflection, Free from desire, one gives rise to joy and bliss;
Tranquil, one enters the first dhyāna, Wherein both internal and external are entirely pure.
The basis and the object Are like a statue of refined gold.
Abiding in the Brahma-world, one finds supreme delight therein.
Furthermore, the fivefold marks are seen: the body and its objects appear;
in the second [dhyāna], applied and sustained thought are extinguished, and the mind is inwardly pure and unified.
The joy and bliss born of concentration manifest within the body through its four factors;
their basis and object are like genuine coral.
In the third station, one is detached from joy, practicing equanimity, mindfulness, and wisdom, and attaining purification.
The body experiences the bliss of samādhi, with the five factors clearly manifest.
Its support is blue lapis lazuli, pure and exceedingly subtle;
conditioned by the small body, it becomes immeasurable, as all the marks arise in succession.
Fourth, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy,
one dwells in equanimity, mindful and pure— this is the third dhyāna.
Such are the characteristics of these four factors, manifesting both the body and the objective sphere.
With the cessation of out-breathing and in-breathing, that upon which they depend becomes utterly pure and white.
Transcending form and the cessation of resistance, this is called entering the sphere of infinite space;
transcending the characteristics of space, one attains the concentration of infinite consciousness; transcending consciousness, there is nothing whatsoever.
Beyond this is nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
skillfully knowing the characteristics of all realms, one neither relishes them nor is bound by them.
The four pure brahma-vihāras are lofty, vast, and immeasurable.
Loving-kindness and compassion pervade everywhere; joy and equanimity are likewise so.
Within the four fundamental dhyānas, one cultivates and gives rise to the five supernormal powers;
when samādhi manifests before one, one binds the mind to contemplate one's own body.
Forming the perception of lightness and softness, raise [the body] gradually without causing it to tremble;
when the object appears before you, leave the ground like a sesame seed;
advance slightly like a barley grain, and successively rise to the height of four finger-breadths.
From this seat to that seat, Gradually able to act as one desires;
Flying through the air and manifesting transformations, Moving with mastery and without obstruction—
This is called the subtle power of supernormal knowledges Of the practitioner.
Fixing the mind upon one's own body, meditative concentration manifests before one;
clearly perceiving external sounds, one hears them all exactly as they are.
Fixing the mind upon one's own body, meditative concentration manifests before one.
Observing the thoughts in the minds of others, he knows them all completely.
Fixing his mind upon his own body, meditative concentration manifests before him;
he recollects this life of his own, from the womb through the intermediate state.
Gradually he beholds the events of his former lives, even those spanning hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
all that he has experienced, he recollects and knows as it truly was.
Fixing his mind upon his own body, meditative concentration manifests before him.
Observing the classes of sentient beings, their births and deaths, and their physical forms,
according to the retribution of their karma, they are born into the five destinies via the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Having cultivated the purity of the divine eye, they see all things exactly as they are.
Within the fundamental stages, there are immeasurable further merits;
through the mastery of mind in practice, all are fully possessed.
These are known as the eight liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality.

There are five characteristics of liberation: the characteristic of impurity, the characteristic of purity, the characteristic of form, affliction, and consciousness; these five characteristics are taught in brief.
Regarding the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): first, with respect to oneself, one perceives internal forms while perceiving external forms that are few;
whether beautiful or ugly, they are regarded as one. The second is likewise, but with external forms that are many.
Then, having no perception of internal form, one externally perceives forms that are few or many.
Whether both are beautiful or ugly, these are the first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
The latter four involve being internally formless while perceiving external forms— blue, yellow, red, and white— and finally,
the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of the four great elements.
The four formless realms, space, and consciousness; contemplating the external and internal body—these are of one mark, without distinction.
The various eloquences, wondrous vows, and wisdoms; the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) and samādhi;
the regressive, progressive, and transcendent modes—the immeasurable gates of samādhi.
With clear wisdom and resolute observation, one is endowed with five kinds of fulfillment:
first, the body; second, the object; third, the pervasive presence of the signs of concentration;
fourth, the fulfillment of mindfulness; and fifth, the cultivation of joy, equanimity, and relinquishment.
The fourth is the fulfillment of all stages, wherein the characteristics of the ten sites are clearly understood;
with the faculties of the three vehicles fully perfected, this is called the fifth fulfillment.
Through the accomplishment of skillful means regarding the realms, the long-standing darkness of ignorance is extinguished.
It can cause the mind to be pure, stainless like space.
All such merits as these are entirely perfected.
The thirteenth chapter, "Contemplating the Elements," is finished.

14. Cultivating the Samādhi of the Four Immeasurables. Chapter Fourteen on Cultivating the Samādhi of the Four Immeasurables. If a practitioner wishes to extensively cultivate the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they should first fix the mind upon its object of focus and gradually practice until it becomes immeasurable.
Having eliminated the mind of transgression and evil, one is free from contention and rivalry, possesses no lingering enmity, and is pure of ill will.

That is to say, toward the three types of beings—friends, neutrals, and enemies—and the nine grades of sentient beings, immeasurable and innumerable, dwelling throughout the ten directions to the very limits of the threefold world, one abides in a state of uniform practice of joy.

Excluding the realm of the physical world, when one universally and collectively takes all sentient beings as the object of focus and achieves the state of a practitioner who dwells in the cultivation of the skillful means of loving-kindness—first contemplating with an even mind, collectively focusing on all sentient beings to make the mind firm, thereby eliminating hatred and giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness—this is called the samādhi of the immeasurable loving-kindness of collective contemplation.

If, despite such general contemplation, one remains bound by hatred, one should cultivate the specific aspect of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward a superior relative. Next, one should sequentially cultivate the nine grades of loving-kindness toward middle relatives, inferior relatives, neutral persons, and enemies. Gradually becoming free from hatred, one gives rise to thoughts of affection and bestows various means of happiness.
Having bestowed this happiness, he then gives rise to a mind that benefits all sentient beings through the Dharma, cultivating three kinds of loving-kindness:
vast loving-kindness, far-reaching loving-kindness, and immeasurable loving-kindness.

Having abandoned and eliminated anger and hindrances, they abide in a heart of benevolence and compassion; according to what is appropriate for their roots of merit and virtue, they bestow upon them all the Buddha-dharmas—namely, granting various kinds of Dharma-joy, practicing various forms of loving-kindness, first granting the joy of renunciation, next the joy of meditative absorption and right attainment, next the joy of enlightenment, and finally the joy of cessation.

Whatever various articles of pleasure that practitioner has previously experienced or not yet experienced—whether acquired by oneself or obtained from others, including pure roots of goodness up to unsurpassed quiescence and ultimate unconditionedness—along with the immeasurable joys of the Dharma corresponding to their practice and mental reflections, appear before them together with the marks of sentient beings.
Once the thought of joy has arisen, one observes each instance individually and realizes it through its own characteristics, thereby attaining certainty.
Just as images appear in a clear mirror because of external objects,
so too does the mirror of the *maitrī-samādhi* manifest all manner of joyful signs before one due to joyful events.
At times, when practicing cultivation, one may be disturbed by anger and think:
"From time immemorial, because of this anger, I have committed many killings and rebellious sins, entering the evil realms and suffering bitter poisons within the great hells;

or I have become bees, scorpions, centipedes, venomous snakes, evil dragons, harmful ghosts, or rākṣasas—various kinds of poisonous and harmful beings—and if I do not eliminate it now, I shall again be tormented and oppressed."
By this expedient means, one can cease anger.
Furthermore, one reflects:
"The one who reviles and the one who receives the reviling—both 'self' and 'other' are impermanent, not abiding for even a moment; both have already passed away."
Once the evil sound has ceased, the two people who subsequently arise have no cause for their mutual dispute.
Furthermore, these two people perish moment by moment; being illusory and without reality, who is it that reviles and who is it that receives the revilement?
Why do you engage in conflict with emptiness through such perversions?

You reckon that your own faculty of hearing arises from false, inverted afflictions and karma; the tongue-faculty of that person is likewise so. Since both arise and perish according to causes and conditions, who is it that reviles, and who is it that hears?
When one practices and reflects in this way, the bonds of anger are severed, and one is able to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), becoming free from defilement and pure.
As the Buddha said:

"One who cultivates loving-kindness can attain decisiveness regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*); through cultivation and expansion, they accomplish immeasurable dharma-gates and the fruits of the sublime path, never again falling back."
This constitutes the great compassion of three kinds of skillful means.

If one has already become free from desire, they further cultivate the pure, wondrous, and desire-free mind of compassion; with a profound intent to benefit others, it increases and expands immeasurably, attaining the fruit of reality.
Because one is thus endowed with these merits, one’s aspirations will culminate in *nirvāṇa*.

Why is this? All Buddhas declare that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is fearlessness; loving-kindness is the mother of all merits; loving-kindness is the fire-drill for producing all merits; and loving-kindness can extinguish all violent evils. Therefore, in practice, one should diligently apply skillful means to cultivate the great loving-kindness that is free from desire.
Regarding immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*): just as with the objects of loving-kindness—enemies, friends, and neutral persons—compassion is practiced in the same sequence.
As the Buddha said:
"Benefiting sentient beings is called the mind of loving-kindness."
"To eliminate what is unbeneficial is called the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*).

If one first gives rise to a mind of benefit toward sentient beings and bestows all manner of happiness upon them, and subsequently observes those beings seeing only the experience of happiness, this is called the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

If one first observes sentient beings undergoing immeasurable suffering and gives rise to a mind that eliminates what is unbeneficial, and subsequently sees those beings having eliminated what is unbeneficial; [this is compassion].
Having removed that which is unbeneficial, one experiences various forms of happiness; this is not the act of bestowing happiness itself, and it is called the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Seeing the sign of purity is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), while seeing the sign of space is compassion;
practicing for the sake of happiness is loving-kindness, while practicing for the sake of suffering is compassion—this is their distinction.
That is to say, when a practitioner sees sentient beings who are fierce, contentious, and enraged; who are cruel, murderous, and harmful;
and who mutually oppress one another without any protection—having seen this, he gives rise to a heart of compassion and acts as their protector.

Furthermore, seeing sentient beings whose bodies, heads, ears, and noses were severed, and whose limbs suffered immeasurable pain with no one to rescue them, the practitioner, having witnessed this, gives rise to a heart of compassion.

Furthermore, when practicing and abiding in a mind of compassion, one sees the sentient beings of the five destinies with their agonizing pains blazing intensely and being tormented by immeasurable distress; thus, one gives rise to deep compassion and conceives the thought of providing rescue and protection.
When such roots of goodness arise through the practice of immeasurable compassion, the signs of immeasurable merit manifest.
If one sees these sentient beings undergoing immeasurable suffering yet fails to give rise to compassion, this person is utterly evil and devoid of roots of goodness.
Such great compassion is that which all Buddhas have practiced from the beginning; by means of it, they have reached the ultimate ocean of omniscience.
If a practitioner can fully cultivate this, one should know that before long they will surely arrive at this state.

Regarding immeasurable joy (*muditā*): it refers to practicing the sphere of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), whereby one uses the various virtuous merits such as the six recollections, the immeasurable qualities of the Buddha-dharma, and all the merits of one's own accomplishment in precepts, concentration, and wisdom, to benefit sentient beings, giving them both one’s own happiness and the happiness of others in their entirety.
Having seen all sentient beings attain the joy of the Dharma, his mind is filled with gladness;
because his mind is glad, his sorrow and distress are extinguished;
once sorrow and distress are extinguished, he becomes consistently joyful, leaping for joy and exulting, thinking, "How wonderful! May they forever abide in peace and happiness."
When one feels joy toward all sentient beings, seeing signs of happiness that are subtle, luminous, and pure, and thereby accomplishing these signs, it is called the Immeasurable Samādhi of Joy.
As the Buddha said:
"Cultivating and accumulating joy and so forth, up to the sphere of consciousness.

Regarding the immeasurable equanimity (*upekṣā*), once one has abandoned [the distinctions between] enemies and kin, one regards with impartiality those of middling quality; these are exclusively sentient beings, without distinction.

Apart from loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, there is only the practice of approaching sentient beings and the characteristic of proximity to their sphere; for this reason, the World-Honored One taught equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Each of the various forms of equanimity has its own specific characteristic, but the immeasurable equanimity is not the same as those others; it is characterized by impartial purity and is free from the marks of suffering and pleasure.
When the appearance of similarity to equanimity arises, this is called the immeasurable samādhi of equanimity.
The World-Honored One taught the cultivation of the immeasurables of equanimity up to the sphere of nothingness.
Having briefly explained the characteristics of these four immeasurables, the practitioner should cultivate their various other profound characteristics in successive order.

15. The Fifteenth Practice: Contemplating the Aggregates (Skandhas). If a practitioner has long accumulated merit and previously practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), even with little instruction, they may awaken their fundamental affinity and be able to contemplate and observe the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Thus they will thoroughly understand the profound Dharma and extinguish birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It is like a great wind dispersing heavy clouds; likewise, they sever all dharmas that Mara delights in.
The meaning of contemplating the five aggregates shall now be explained.

The practitioner reflects within himself, desiring to cross the ocean of afflictions; he gives rise to detachment from desire, produces moisture, experiences personal bliss, and the coarse and rough four great elements are extinguished.
In accordance with the arising of the four great elements, one gathers all distracted thoughts, is able to proceed toward the ultimate, and accomplishes wisdom.

If the locus of fundamental contemplation is firm, stable, and luminously pure, one can give rise to samādhi, depart from all distracted conceptions, extinguish afflictions, and all subtle and wondrous signs will then fully manifest.

Like pure and exquisite lapis lazuli, or like a clear bubble of water, the practitioner perceives this arising of a luminous, pure, and stainless mark; maintaining it with wholesome mindfulness, the mind does not become negligent.
Once there is no negligence, the mark of maturation arises.
Once the characteristic of maturation has arisen, the characteristic of decay appears;
once the characteristic of decay has appeared, one gives rise only to the perception of phenomena, wherein all things are utterly tranquil and extinguished.
By thus practicing the characteristics of phenomena and fully accomplishing them, one attains a superior sense of weary detachment.
With firm and unshakable diligence, he attains the profound samādhi, the firm samādhi, and the immovable samādhi.
Abiding in the cultivation of these samādhis, he is able to give rise to five kinds of pure and luminous samādhis that universally illumine the five realms of existence:
the moonlight samādhi, the sunlight samādhi, the pure lapis lazuli samādhi, the refined golden light samādhi, and the stainless crystal samādhi.
Therefore, from these five kinds of pure samādhis, there further arise the Samādhi of Radiance, the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, and the Samādhi of Immeasurable Radiance.
Furthermore, the practitioner, by means of the five signs of decay, is able to destroy all conditions:
first, piercing; second, peeling; third, splitting; fourth, breaking; and fifth, extinction.
By means of these five marks of disintegration, one disintegrates all phenomena.
Having cultivated the five kinds of samādhis and purified all objective spheres, there subsequently arise five kinds of samādhi-marks:
the Lion King Samādhi, the Dragon King Samādhi, the Garuḍa King Samādhi, the Ox King Samādhi, and the Elephant King Samādhi.
Because his mind is free from negligence, he manifests this heroic form.
By practicing and abiding in this King of Beasts Samādhi, he gathers all beings within their respective categories.
Furthermore, through the power of samādhi, the ten marks of male and female arise; according to their respective types, they encompass one another, and all sentient beings appear therein.
If one can discern these various marks of samādhi without fear, this is called the merit of mastery over all dharmas.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes within the luminous and pure realm how the flow of the aggregates (skandhas) emerges from a single place and divides into two parts.
Having observed this, they again merge back into one.
Within each individual stream, five further signs are seen;
these signs are distinct from one another and are arrayed as objective fields.
Once they have been arrayed as objective fields, they again merge back into one.

Form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a water bubble, perception is viewed as a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is viewed as an illusion; these five are false and deceptive in nature.
Having practiced such contemplation, his body becomes peaceful, supple, and blissful.
He further contemplates the place where the flow originates; a stainless mark appears, like a pure bubble on water, which gradually increases in size until it fills his entire body.
Practicing with a mind free from negligence, one focuses the mindfulness to receive and uphold [the signs].
Having upheld them, the pure marks increase and expand, pervading and covering the entire body; like clear and pure bubbles, they are free from all faults and evils.
When a more excellent and wondrous wisdom arises, it destroys this mark;
once the mark is destroyed, that flow descends and pours forth distantly in immeasurable streams, like pure crystal, reaching the ultimate sphere of knowledge.
Having reached the ultimate sphere of knowledge, one withdraws from that state and forms a maṇḍala.

Furthermore, there are other extraordinary signs that fill their original locations; subsequently, they flow out to reach immeasurable worlds in the ten directions. Having reached the ten directions, each abides in its own characteristic.
At that time, the practitioner clearly perceives immeasurable varieties of form, which are like masses of foam drifting and accumulating in mountain streams;
all characteristics of sensation are like bubbles from heavy raindrops;
and various perceptions are like mirages in the springtime.
The formations are like the plantain tree, lacking any solid core;
one contemplates the seeds of the six consciousnesses as being like illusions and transformations.
Such various kinds of falsehoods merely deceive the foolish; this is called the practice of contemplating the specific characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Having observed the specific characteristics of the aggregates, one further uses wisdom to illuminate one's own body, observing with focused mindfulness.
While observing, one sees that the place where the body arises is ablaze all around; within it are various kinds of miscellaneous flowers, pure and wondrous, and precious jewels encircling the body.
Furthermore, one sees one's own body adorned with various miscellaneous jewels and marks of merit, subtle and magnificent.
Having practiced and seen these various marks, his eye of wisdom opened wide; looking back at his own body, he observed it thoroughly.

Having completed this observation, he further looked outward at the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), which were like a blazing, raging fire. He immediately conceived a mind of revulsion, applying himself with courageous diligence, desiring to cross the boundless ocean of suffering of birth and death.

Having cultivated the perception of the five aggregates as burning and having become weary of them, the perception of dispassion, the perception of liberation, the perception of nirvana, and the perception of all meritorious qualities arise in succession.
Furthermore, the practitioner possesses the sevenfold contemplation, observing the five aggregates, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

He further contemplates how the five aggregates arise from craving, and through weariness with them, seeks renunciation; thus, within the true truths, the wisdom of the seeds of skillful means is born.
Thus, having well cultivated the three types of contemplation regarding these seven bases, the contemplation of specific characteristics is accomplished;
once this has been achieved with certainty and firmness, one subsequently attains the stainless cultivation of wisdom through cessation.
When this wisdom arises, its objects are balanced and upright, pure and unmixed.

Furthermore, having attained the resolute contemplation of superior, wondrous, and stainless wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), one perceives the rise and fall of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and their moment-by-moment dissolution, thereby seeing their true nature.
It is like poisoned rice: whoever eats it will surely die;
likewise, that which is mixed with the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates when one practices this contemplation is also of such a nature.
When a thought arises, it is suffering; at the very moment of that single thought, it arises, abides, and ceases.
When that thought arises, it arises simultaneously with suffering.
Therefore, in a single thought-moment, that very thought-moment perishes.

When one practices the contemplation of the five aggregates in this way—seeing them as subject to arising and ceasing, destruction, falsehood, impermanence, and evil—one immediately gives rise to the practice of impermanence, the practice of suffering, the practice of emptiness and stillness, and the practice of non-self; [one perceives them as] phenomena that are leaking, unreal, rapidly decaying, and subject to disintegration.
Such is the meaning of impermanence, as explained at length in the sūtras, even up to a hundred phrases.
By practicing and fully cultivating all such characteristics, one comes to know the reality of all phenomena and thereby attains liberation.

By practicing the contemplation of the samādhi of the stage of the noble ones, one observes this mark of impermanence; thereupon, profound sorrow and weariness arise, and seeing the faults and afflictions of the conditioned, one takes no pleasure in the three realms of existence.
Furthermore, if a practitioner contemplates arising as not ceasing, or contemplates ceasing as not arising, they will not give rise to the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*).
Only when the mind is single-pointed and of a single characteristic, correctly directed toward liberation, does wisdom arise; this is the definitive noble practice.

Once the noble practice has arisen, all characteristics of phenomena are extinguished without remainder; delusion, craving, afflictions, and all stains of transgression—which cause the aggregates of suffering to revolve—are entirely eliminated.
Once [the afflictions] have been extinguished, the mind is tamed; this is the vision that the five aggregates are without self and without what belongs to a self (*anātman* and *anātmīya*).

By observing impermanent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as suffering, one observes the aggregate of suffering as being oppressed by the eight types of suffering, thereby accomplishing the eight modes of practice regarding these eight aspects of suffering.

That which is called being like a disease, like an abscess, like a thorn, like a murderer, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—these four are noble practices and four are non-noble practices; one is resolute regarding the aggregate of suffering and contemplates its reality.
These four truths and sixteen noble practices constitute the initial mark of cultivating the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Within the ground of the true truths, one attains authentic wisdom.
One contemplates the aggregate of suffering as being like a glowing iron ball—devoid of solidity—and turns toward *nirvāṇa* while turning away from *saṃsāra*;
one no longer prizes existence and takes no delight in birth.
It is like a herd of wild animals surrounded by hunters; driven by the urgency of their fear, they leap forth with courageous speed.
So it is with spiritual practice: seeing that birth and death are ablaze and besieged by great suffering, one transcends them without obstruction through the power of the wisdom of revulsion.
Furthermore, when the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) arises in the practitioner, the seed of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) emerges;

when the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) arises through the practice of cessation (*śamatha*), the seed of heat increases, reaches its own stage, and the characteristics of heat become fully perfected.
When the wisdom cultivated through the practice of cessation arises, the seeds of the "Summit" (mūrdhan) dharma emerge;
when the "Heat" (uṣmagata) dharma arises, the seeds of the Summit increase;
upon reaching the Summit itself, the characteristics of the Summit become fully perfected.
When the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata) arises, the seeds of Patience (kṣānti) emerge;
when the stage of Summits (mūrdhan) arises, the seeds of Patience increase;
upon reaching the stage of Patience itself, the characteristics of Patience become fully perfected.
Furthermore, finding delight in the five aggregates is called the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
Contemplating the five aggregates and finding delight in the Three Jewels is called the stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan).

Contemplating the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) during the stage of the Peak Dharma (*mūrdha-dharma*), one finds joy and approval regarding the Four Noble Truths; this is called the stage of Patience (*kṣānti-dharma*).

During the stage of Patience, one contemplates the twelve bases (*āyatana*); as both [stages] contemplate all three types [of suffering], yet differ because one specific root of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) becomes predominant, they are said to have distinctions.

All these observe the ultimate truth; however, in the stage of Patience (kṣānti), the observation of reality increases; in the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata), the perception increases; in the stage of Summits (mūrdhan), faith, observation, and joy increase; and in the stage of Patience, wisdom increases.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of conditions for practice: namely, the upper, the lower, and the various directions.
Based on these three conditions, the three kinds of roots of goodness each attain a state of predominance; therefore, it is said that they bring about satisfaction (the original text says "xuanshe").

Furthermore, the three types of cultivation of *ūṣmagata* (heat) rely respectively on revulsion toward the summit (*mūrdhan*), on contemplation of joy (*kṣānti*), and on equanimity (*upekṣā*). Since they also follow the single increase of those roots of goodness, it should be known that one type of cultivation brings them all to completion, thereby accomplishing these three dharmas.
Furthermore, practitioners should know this!
It is like a person who has five enemy bandits following him with drawn swords, constantly seeking to harm him;
the successive oppression and逼迫 (coercion) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) from before to after is exactly like this.
The Buddha said:
"Those who seek *anabhisaṃskāra*—this is a name for the Path of Vision—should practice *dharmamanasikāra*.

Constantly contemplate the true meaning and, with the sword of noble conduct, sever the thieves of the aggregates (*skandha*). Do not be like an inferior man who, unable to grasp a staff, is harmed by them."

All worthy and holy ones should likewise diligently cultivate such right contemplation for the sake of happiness in the present life, for the sake of creating great illumination for future lives, for the sake of severing the root of all suffering, and for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
How much more so for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), who, being empty and having nothing to attain, are self-indulgent and do not diligently practice.
Having completed the contemplation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Dharmamaṇasagāra:
*Dharma* means "phenomenon," referring here to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
*Manasikāra* means "having once passed through the mind"; the translator’s gloss explains it as "contemplation" (*cintā*).

16. The Sixteenth Chapter on the Practice of Contemplating the Entrances: The six entrances each bind ignorant sentient beings to their respective objects; because of a mind of craving desire, they constantly give rise to perceptions of purity.

Practitioners should know that regarding the objects of the sense faculties, they must restrain what is unwholesome, collect the mind upon its focal object so that it remains unmoving, and correctly contemplate the six sense bases.

For example, like an empty village, it is devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self," and thus lacks a fixed meaning; it has the sense of being a locus of entry and the sense of dragging one downward. This sense of being a locus of entry can lead sentient beings into the evil realms.
Furthermore, as for the characteristics of the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), they are like glowing iron spikes, like an extremely sharp sword, and also like a keen blade.
The Buddha said:
"If one contemplates these characteristics, one will be able to relinquish them."
Furthermore, one contemplates that the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*) are like evil bandits who plunder the precious treasures of goodness.
If one practices the abandonment of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), opening the gates of the sense entrances and allowing the six objects to run wild,
then the evil bandits of the six objects will plunder pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and cause one to lose all meritorious qualities (*guṇa*).
It is like a bird that wishes to fly through the sky without two wings, or a person who wishes to travel afar without two feet.

Practice is likewise: because one has destroyed the merit of the pure precepts, the two wings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* will never grow again, and thus one can never hope to transcend birth and death.

Just as water held in a broken jar does not remain for even a moment, so it is with a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts: the water of the dharma of samādhi does not abide within him for even an instant.
Just as the celestial vase of merit, when guarded and not broken, constantly produces precious jewels inexhaustibly according to one's wishes;
so too is it with spiritual practice: if one does not violate the pure precepts, one will constantly give birth to the jewels of noble merit.
If the vessel of virtue is lightly damaged, its precious contents will immediately perish;
if the vessel of precepts is broken, one will forever lose the treasure of the Dharma.

It is like a person whose nose has been cut off: when looking in a mirror, they find no joy. A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is just the same; when he examines himself within, his heart finds no pleasure.
Just as the hundred grains and medicinal trees grow depending upon the earth, so all virtuous merits depend entirely upon pure precepts.
As sandalwood paste applied to the body can remove heat and affliction,
so pure precepts, being cool and refreshing, can extinguish the fire of desire.
Just as a wish-fulfilling gem becomes cool wherever it is placed when it is hot, so too is pure ethical discipline:
within the fire of the afflictions, it is able to extinguish the blazing heat.

A bhikṣu who has violated the precepts reflects that his transgression is grave; when his body perishes and his life ends, he will inevitably enter the evil realms. His mind is constantly filled with sorrow and regret, and he is terrified at the time of death.
A person of pure precepts is always joyful in mind; they have no sorrow or regret in life and experience peace and happiness at the time of death.
Pure precepts serve as a ladder by which one can ascend to the hall of wisdom.
Precepts are an ornament, and they are also a virtuous guard;
precepts can lead a person to nirvana.
Precepts are the fertile ground from which the seeds of the ten wholesome actions sprout.

The water of the teacher’s instruction irrigates them at the proper times, whereby the root of faith takes birth. The aggregates of outflowlessness (*anāsrava-skandha*) serve as the trunk; the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the sprouts; the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) is the branches; having few desires and knowing contentment are the twigs and leaves; the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are the flowers; the wisdom of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*) is the fruit; and the dharma of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) is the ambrosia (*amṛta*).
The fragrance of the precepts flows forth, universally perfuming all.
The noble and holy bird-kings dwell and rest therein;
