compassion serves as a heavy canopy, providing vast, cool coverage.
The Dharma Master of Eloquence was the king of the bees; with harmonious voices and mutual regard, they would always gather the refined essences.
That tree was tall and straight, firm, solid, and substantial, being free from falsehood, flattery, crookedness, or decay; thus it was called the Great Tree of Merit.

All practitioners who wish to proceed toward nirvāṇa turn their backs on the suffering of the three periods of time and head toward the city of liberation. Gradually practicing and giving rise to all virtuous merits, they rest beneath that tree, drink the nectar of the Dharma, and quench the affliction of the three cravings; with their bodies at peace, they are able to reach nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the precepts have many numerical categories: they may be one, two, three, or four; or seven, or twelve, or twenty-one.

If, in every thought-moment and for even a brief instant, there are immeasurable seeds of precepts—namely, the precepts co-arising with the Path, those co-arising with meditative concentration, and innate precepts; as well as right speech, right action, and right livelihood—they revolve together with the mind.
Contemplating these various precepts, their characteristics are each distinct: some are pure and stainless, while others are light and luminously clear;
thus, the characteristic of stainless precepts manifests within the objective field.

In practicing the contemplation based on mindfulness, one observes the characteristics of the precepts in three locations: if the ointments are soft, free from impurities, delightful, bright, pure, and white, these are the characteristics within the locus of support;

if the ground is level and vast, adorned with exquisite flowers, precious vessels, and ornaments, and the various jewels are smooth and lustrous, these are called the characteristics within the sphere of practice.
It is like a yak that guards its tail: if a single hair becomes caught in a tree, it will rather die clinging to the tree than allow the hair to break.
A bhikṣu who guards the precepts is just like this; even for the sake of death, he will not violate a single minute precept.
His wondrous marks adorn his body and his secondary characteristics are fully complete, like the autumn moon shining steadily in the void.

Having practiced samādhi and contemplated this mark of purity, until the end of one's life, there is no further anxiety or regret, nor is there any feverish distress; one is no longer terrified, but instead experiences peace, joy, and delight, with exultation increasing and the bliss of tranquility arising, while the coarse and harsh four great elements are extinguished—these and others like them are called the marks within the practice of mindfulness.
Furthermore, within these three types there are further mixed characteristics that cause agitation, obstruction, loss of mindfulness, and instability of mind.

One should request forgiveness for past transgressions and unwholesome evil karma, vowing never to commit them again even unto death; thus, one remains free from offense even in dreams, further increasing and strengthening the observance of the precepts.
The Buddha said:
"Precepts are like flower garlands and scented ointments, the ornaments that adorn one;
while the fragrance of incense coming from a single direction is the scent of worldly things, the fragrance of the virtue of precepts comes from all directions."
Or their bodies may lack hands, feet, eyes, ears, noses, or tongues, with all their limbs and joints incomplete;
or their bodies may be submerged in dust and grime;
or they may observe themselves as free from all defilement, bathing and anointing their bodies, clad in renowned garments and superior robes—this is called cultivation.
Regarding the observation of mindfulness based on conditions, there are various aspects of ethical discipline (*śīla*), including its diverse characteristics and modes of conduct.

The three types of discipline—those concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and those concomitant with the Path (*mārga*)—have all been explained herein. Furthermore, there are immeasurable other profound and subtle characteristics, which the wise should expound upon in detail.

Having practiced and contemplated pure precepts, one who wishes to shatter the mountains of the sense bases (*āyatana*) should cultivate two dharmas: namely, *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

First, one should contemplate the joy of detachment from evil, which fills the body; the coarse and harsh four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are extinguished, and the supple and compliant four great elements arise. One proceeds toward the bliss of tranquil cessation, with a single mind undisturbed.
When one fixes the mind upon the sign of entering within one's own body, one should skillfully guard the locus from which that sign of entering arises.
When observing, if a pure and bright sign arises, the bhikṣu, seeing this sign, should skillfully guard it as the Buddha has taught.
Just as a brooding hen who protects her chicks well will surely achieve success,
so too it is with a bhikṣu’s practice: by guarding it with single-minded diligence, he achieves success,
and the signs of the twelve fruits of cultivation appear clearly.
When practicing with diligent protection, one is free from all negligence;
when the fruit of practice is accomplished, the objective realm is pure and sublime, devoid of all defilement.

It is as bright as a precious gem and like a suspended stream of water; the objective realm is vast and full, while the body occupies but a small portion, flowing out everywhere to distant reaches and then returning back again.
Having returned, a single mark appears; it then divides into two parts, which again merge into one to form the realm of the maṇḍala.
It abides in perfect equilibrium, universally manifesting various marks like the radiance of a multitude of stars arrayed in formation, and only thereafter does it dissolve.
Once it has been destroyed, each part flows out and merges back into one;
it then flows far and wide in all directions, filling every quarter;
having filled all quarters, it returns once more to abide peacefully and firmly.
Once it has settled, the signs of ripening appear;

once the signs of ripening have appeared, various manifold characteristics emerge, becoming pervasive and expansive, with all manner of exquisite vessels, garments, and extraordinary features manifesting.

The internal sense bases within the objective sphere are an empty village; external forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and the three types of phenomena across the three periods of time—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—all manifest therein, and one contemplates their true reality.

Furthermore, the six external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*) are like thieves, and the six internal sense bases (*adhyātmāyatana*) are like an empty village. It is also taught that these internal and external bases constitute this shore and the other shore.
These various excellent and sublime characteristics of the twelve bases are immeasurably vast and extensive, as the Buddha has explained at length in the *Sūtras*.

Furthermore, as the practitioner cultivates, the characteristic of ripening arises within this objective field; having arisen, it again disintegrates. From time to time, there are characteristics of interruption and separation, and these characteristics of interruption and separation flow forth to an extreme distance, remaining fixed in one place.
It is like a precious vessel filled with water; when it is subsequently opened, one gradually perceives tranquility;
once tranquility is attained, all other various marks of merit then arise.
From within the various gateways, the characteristics of mutual interpenetration constantly flow forth; once each has emerged, they again form a maṇḍala in a single location.
Upon this maṇḍala, the characteristics of self-nature further arise;
having arisen, they mature, and having matured, they soon enter into quiescent extinction.
Thereafter, as the practitioner continues to cultivate with even greater diligence, further pure and subtle signs of dhyāna appear; having appeared, they sequentially subside and cease as before.

Furthermore, within the various sense bases (*āyatana*), there arise various wondrous signs at the locus where the mind is bound, giving rise to a definitive sign known as the Samādhi of the Bright Jewel in the Topknot.
In practice, one contemplates one's own body as divided into two parts, with a precious lotus flower atop a treasury of various jewels;
in practice, one sees one's own body upon that lotus flower, surrounded by a magnificent array of various precious flowers.
Furthermore, as the Blessed One stated in the Sūtras regarding the six similes of sentient beings, the practitioner should observe them fully.
That is to say: the eye is like a dog, running after the village of five colors;
the ear is like a bird, taking flight upon hearing sounds in the sky.
The nose is a venomous serpent,
ever following the nostrils;
the tongue is a jackal, greedily coveting the corpses of the five flavors.
The body is like a *śūcīmukha* worm, always delighting in entering the ocean of contact;
the mind is like a monkey, always delighting in roaming through the forest of dharmas across the three periods of time.
If these six types of sentient beings were bound to a single place, they would not be able to roam freely where they please.

Practicing in this manner, one binds the six sense faculties with samādhi and right mindfulness so that they do not wander freely toward their objects; thereafter, one contemplates the reality of phenomena with pure wisdom.

Ignorant and deluded ordinary beings, amidst the six sense objects, greedily cling to and long for immeasurable unwholesome dharmas. Contemplating them correctly in this way, one can completely eliminate all sentient beings' attachment to sense objects, which creates obstacles that prevent them from reaching nirvana.
Therefore, those who practice the path wishing to destroy birth and death and proceed toward nirvana should subdue their sense faculties and remain far removed from sensory objects.

Chapter Seventeen: The Practice of Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Having already explained the various remedies and the factors to be remedied, the remedy for delusion should now be analyzed.
The dependent origination taught by all Buddhas eliminates the darkness of ignorance and gives rise to knowledge of reality as it is.
It possesses profound, subtle, and conformable merits, which I shall now briefly explain so that the merits of all practitioners may increase and their delusion be extinguished.
Observing dependent origination, one distances oneself from all conceptualizations of the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;

knowing that conditioned phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, one is also able to subdue and lead the deluded and intoxicated followers of external paths to accord with the supreme dharma of emptiness. Thus, the eye of wisdom becomes clear and pure, and ignorance is entirely extinguished.
There are four types of contemplation on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
first, continuous bondage; second, flowing succession; third, segmented division; and fourth, momentariness.
Continuous bondage has six aspects:
First is birth, second is division, third is destination, fourth is the gate of birth, fifth is the moment, and sixth is formation and destruction. Regarding birth:
from the aggregates of death, the intermediate state (antarābhava) subsequently arises;
from the intermediate state, the aggregates of birth subsequently arise.
Beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are clouded by ignorance and blinded by folly; they perform karma that leads to existence.
When these beings see a man and woman in union, because their ignorance has increased, they give rise to perverted perceptions: either thoughts of hostility, or thoughts of affection.
Those who desire to be with a woman conceive thoughts of hostility toward the man, and then perceive themselves in union with her.
At that time, being deluded and intoxicated by desire is called arising from craving;
seeing impurity yet perceiving it as one's own is called arising from pride;
growing through the mother’s food and drink, causing the body to develop and emerge, is called arising from nutriment.
When the four great elements arise together with the kalala, they obtain the retribution-body; this is called the arising of the body from the four great elements.
With the karma of bondage as the expedient means, once these two stages have passed, the seed of consciousness arises in succession; this is called the seed-consciousness.
When first dwelling in the *kalala* stage, the mind is submerged, with little consciousness and dull, unsharp awareness; this is called being born as a *kalala*.
Because it has already discerned with clarity and acuity, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); this is what is meant by the "continuity of birth.

As for "segmentation," from the *kalala*, there successively arise the *arbuda*, the *peśī*, the solid mass, the limbs and joints, infancy, childhood, youth, maturity, the stage of decline, and the stage of old age; this is what is meant by the "continuity of segmentation."
"Destinies" (gati) refers to reaching all destinies and practicing the contemplation of the characteristics of those destinies; this is called the "bondage of destinies.
"Gateways of birth" (yoni-mukha) refers to the continuity of the four modes of birth, wherein saṃsāra flows without interruption; this is called the "bondage of the gateways of birth."

Regarding "moment" (*kṣaṇa*): observing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as they continue from moment to moment, with arising and ceasing occurring without interruption—this is called the "succession of moments.

Regarding "formation and destruction": the arising and ceasing of all objective realms, and the beginning and end of kalpas; practicing the contemplation of this continuity of formation and destruction is called the "succession of formation and destruction."
This is the practice of contemplating the continuous bondage of dependent origination.

As for "streaming forth" (pravāha), it refers to the practice of contemplating the flow from a single moment (kṣaṇa) through a tatkṣaṇa, up to a lava and a muhūrta; this is called the stage of the streaming kalala.
The continuous flow for seven days—through the stages of the bubble, the fleshy mass, the hardening and thickening, up to the stage of old age—is called "continuous flow" (*pravāha*).

The stage of arising, the stage of abiding, the stage of the conditions for arising, the stage of entry, the stage of exit, and the stage of skillful means—all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that flow with skillful means, arising and ceasing in succession—are called "continuous flow."
The revolving of the various realms of existence is like a whirling firebrand; this is called "flowing current.
To contemplate all such immeasurable flowing currents in this manner is the practice of observing dependent origination.

Regarding the "flowing succession" and "segmentation": through the practice of contemplative observation, one proceeds from segment to segment; thus it is said that by being able to know segmentation in this way, one achieves mastery over dependent origination.
This means that with ignorance as the predominant condition, one is like a blind person who lacks the faculty of vision; it is like a great, pitch-black darkness, far removed from light.
To have no vision either in front or behind is to be partially blind;
if there is no vision both in front and behind, one is doubly blind.
If one is freed from these two forms of blindness, one abandons the darkness of delusion and attains the bright, pure eye of wisdom.
Thus, ignorance regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, as well as regarding the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, is called the ten kinds of delusion;
the extinction of these ten kinds of delusion is called the ten kinds of wisdom.
The Buddha taught that ignorance is the primary cause, which plants the three kinds of karma.
If one practices without knowing the faults and afflictions of ignorance, one plants these three kinds of karma.
Once karma has arisen, from it consciousness is born; all consciousnesses are like illusions, manifesting in all their various forms.
From the continuity of consciousness, name-and-form arises; within that single body, there are two aspects.
It is like a soft, moist, and decaying object containing various insects that cause it to move and shake from the outside;
or like a wild silkworm first forming its cocoon membrane.
The two characteristics of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are likewise so.
Until the sense-faculties (*indriya*) have been formed, they are called the two characteristics of name-and-form;
once the sense-faculties have opened, it is called the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
When the sense-faculties first open, one has not yet begun to act; one is deluded regarding contact and does not know what is agreeable or disagreeable.
Just as bubbles arise when raindrops fall upon water, so too do feelings arise from contact:
when external thorns prick the body, contact arises from within.
It is also like a lamp made from oil and a wick; this is called the practice of contemplating the characteristic of touch (*sparśa*).
Once the characteristic of touch has arisen, feeling (*vedanā*) arises in succession.
Just as with a bubble of water, three characteristics appear; yet, if one discriminates the various faculties, there are five types of feeling.
Once sensation has arisen, craving subsequently arises.
For example, it is like a tongue licking honey smeared upon the edge of a blade; the increase of craving and the various afflictions is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
From clinging, existence (*bhava*) subsequently arises. There are three kinds of karma; because karma gives rise to future fruit, it is called "existence."
That which has already been planted as birth but has not yet been experienced is called "future birth"; once it has arisen and matured, it is termed "aging and death.
When these two links are spoken of in relation to the time of future birth, the characteristic of birth is predominant.
The Buddha taught that when the constituent of consciousness arises in the future, it is called "birth";
name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are called "old age and death."
Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) in a previous life can accumulate the present existence, they are considered "past" in relation to this life.
Since craving and grasping belong to the category of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are designated as ignorance (*avidyā*);
whereas existence is [equivalent to] volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Now, the three branches from the present can produce future births, while the two branches from the past turn the wheel of birth and death.
Those sentient beings revolve because they are shrouded by ignorance.
Eight belong to the present, two to the past, and two to the future; through this distinction of time periods, one should know that when analyzed in this way, all [factors] are twelvefold.
Furthermore, there is another set of causal factors which I shall now explain.

One contemplates dependent origination through these ten stages: from the kalala, the arbuda, the peśī, the ghana, the praśākhā, the stage of infancy, childhood, youth, the stage of decline, and the stage of old age and death.

Furthermore, regarding the stages of arising, abiding, and the conditions for arising, as well as the phases of entry and exit, and even all other phases, one contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in its entirety.

Furthermore, because this arises, that arises; that is to say, the eye and visible forms give rise to visual consciousness, and through the conjunction of these three factors, contact arises, from which feeling, perception, and volition are produced. This is called the practice of contemplating dependent origination through diverse modes.

Furthermore, practicing skillful means, one contemplates the dependent origination of the sense bases (*āyatana*). By means of a clear and pure objective realm, one directs oneself toward contemplating the gates of the sense bases;
having seen them thus, one individually contemplates their specific characteristics, thereby shattering the mountains of the sense bases and their immeasurable accumulations.
Once these matured signs appear, they flow forth throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the sphere of ultimate wisdom, one reaches it through observation; for those who advance with clear intelligence, they cultivate and abide in skillful means (*upāya*).

At that time, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation arise in succession through the signs of maturation and the signs of disintegration. As for all other advancements, their meaning is as explained previously in the section on "entrances" (*praveśa*).
Furthermore, because this exists, that exists;
because this arises, that arises.
That is to say, the practitioner first breaks down the internal body and subsequently contemplates external forms.
It is just as when looking into a mirror, images appear because of objects;
likewise, when the characteristics of the basis arise, external characteristics also arise.

Furthermore, regarding the practice of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one first fixes the mind firmly upon the preliminary stage (*upāya*) to establish its causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and subsequently analyzes the limbs and joints to observe their causal origination.
Once the appearance of light has arisen, the appearance of ignorance is destroyed.

Relying upon the bones of the feet, there arise the shinbones, thighbones, hipbones, shoulder bones, neck bones, and skull bones, filling the ten directions. The signs of tainted karma appear everywhere, and beneath them, various impure signs arise in successive stages.
Furthermore, one practices the contemplation that four causes can give rise to manifold sufferings:
the indirect cause (*pāramparyahetu*), the proximate cause (*sāmantakahetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*), and the specific cause (*asādhāraṇahetu*).
Furthermore, one practices the contemplation of the arising of effects: birth arises from becoming; becoming arises from grasping; and so on, down to volitional formations arising from ignorance.
Volitional formations are both effects and causes;
inferring the effect from the cause, it is the same when tracing back to old age and death.
If one seeks a cause for ignorance, one will inevitably experience great terror and give rise to the view of annihilationism.
Lacking wisdom and shrouded in darkness, his remaining light is extremely faint, like that of a firefly.
Thus, even as he continues to seek causes without ceasing, he perceives himself as being accompanied only by great, profound darkness.
The World-Honored One said:
"Due to improper mental attention, if sentient beings are accompanied by it, they revolve in birth and death.
Bound by ignorance, the wheel of existence turns perpetually.
With ignorance as the root, the functions of the remaining links each manifest their respective characteristics.
Within the wheel of all the links of existence, ignorance is the most sovereign.

Driven by its sovereign power, it is like a slave belonging to his master. Because this [ignorance] does not exist, there is no activity; because it is extinguished, there is no turning. One should know that the other links are all explained in the same way.
There are four kinds of death:
gradual death, sudden death, death through the exhaustion of karma, and momentary death.
Furthermore, three kinds of impermanence are taught:
First, momentary impermanence; second, segmental impermanence; third, categorical impermanence.
By practicing and realizing this impermanence, one distances oneself from the four māras, destroys ignorance, and the marks of clarity manifest.
Just as a bright and pure lamp can dispel all darkness, so too, when old age and death are extinguished and all luminous signs arise, it is likewise.
Having destroyed ignorance and all its accumulations, one achieves the single characteristic of the pure and wondrous realm.
The practitioner’s body becomes supple and radiant; once it is radiant, the body becomes exceedingly clear and pure, like a reflection in a bright mirror.
When such signs appear with clarity and purity, one observes the various internal components within one's own body, and each of their individual characteristics manifests distinctly.
When such contemplation is accomplished, it is called "attaining transcendence regarding the elements.
Why is this? Because there are five kinds of delusion and five corresponding counteractive characteristics.
First, the elements (*dhātu*); second, the sense bases (*āyatana*); third, the aggregates (*skandha*); fourth, the base and lowly; fifth, defilement—these are called the five kinds of delusion.

Alternatively, those who attain liberation by contemplating the elements, or again, those who attain liberation by contemplating the aggregates, the sense bases, the increase of merit therein, or the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—these are called the five kinds of remedies.
Furthermore, when the practitioner enters the *vaiḍūrya-svaccha-viśuddha-samādhi*, they contemplate the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) within the realm of luminous purity.
While contemplating these branches of dependent origination, the perception that they are easily seen arises, as has been described.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“Is dependent origination easy to see?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The twelvefold dependent origination is profoundly deep and bottomless, difficult to see and difficult to know.

You wish to destroy my fruit—which was attained over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, is profound, subtle, and difficult to obtain—yet why do you joyfully claim that this is a profound and subtle contemplation?"
I shall now deliver you; you should follow me and observe the realm of the Buddha.
Adrift upon the ocean of the Buddha’s realm are the outsiders, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, deluded by the two extremes, and unable to enter the sphere of *tathatā* (suchness).
"Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are able to enter it slightly, they cannot reach its bottom.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he immediately entered the profound, subtle, and wondrous *jñāna-arcis-vihāra-samādhi-svatantra-samāpatti*.

In the realm of right concentration, there are three lion kings; atop each lion king is a pond made of the seven treasures, and within each seven-treasure pond is a lotus flower made of the seven treasures. Upon each of these seven-treasure lotus flowers sits a Buddha, emitting great radiance that reaches the limit of the śrāvaka realm, after which they come to abide.
All the roots of goodness planted by these śrāvakas from their initial aspiration until their final bodies, as well as all their dependent originations, appeared there in their entirety.

From this, three lion kings further arose; upon each lion king was a pond made of the seven treasures, and within each seven-treasure pond was a lotus flower made of the seven treasures. Upon each seven-treasure lotus flower sat a Buddha, emitting great radiance that extended to the limits of the realm of pratyekabuddhas, and only then did they come to rest.
All the roots of goodness planted by the Pratyekabuddhas from their initial aspiration until their ultimate attainment, as well as all their dependent originations, appeared there in their entirety.

From these, there further arose immeasurable lion kings; upon each lion king was a pond made of the seven treasures, and within each seven-treasure pond were seven-treasure lotuses. Upon every single flower sat a Buddha, universally emitting light that reached the ultimate limit of the Bodhisattva realm, after which they came to abide.

All the roots of goodness, all merits, whether karma or its fruits, as well as all dependent originations cultivated by these bodhisattvas from their first aspiration until they reach the Diamond Seat, are all manifested therein.

From this, there further arose immeasurable lion kings; upon each lion king was a pond made of the seven treasures, and within each seven-treasure pond were lotus flowers made of the seven treasures. Upon every single flower sat a Buddha, emitting great radiance that universally illumined the Buddha-dharma and manifested all the most profound dependent origination.
At that time, after the Buddha had revealed the realm of the Buddhas to Ānanda through his supernormal power, he said to Ānanda:

"Within this flame there are further immeasurable and boundless realms of the Buddhas, which are the sphere of the Buddha's wisdom. How can you speak of such a profound and subtle realm as being easy to see with such delight?"
Your wisdom is shallow and insufficient; you merely think it is easy to perceive.
Once the immeasurable dharmas of the *eryan* realm have appeared before you as described above, they subsequently perish, and all become empty, pure, and quiescent.
After they have become quiescent, one further contemplates their supreme excellence.
Thus, as the flames arise, the Buddha’s Dharma-body gradually expands and becomes vast, pervading and filling the ten directions;
immeasurable Dharma-treasures fill this Dharma-body.
The radiance of the Dharma-body is without limit or boundary; it is the sphere of activity of unshared wisdom.
All the profound dependent origination of the Buddha-dharmas manifests before one, and only then do they dissolve; all are empty, pure, and quiescent, having no location;
they are like space, with nothing upon which to rely.
Just as when a jewel enters one's hand, it is called "attaining the jewel";
so it is with the cultivation of the fruit—it is called the "definitive mark. Ānanda!
"The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; I have now shown you but a small portion of it.
Seeing the realm of the Buddha, Ānanda was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and he addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is most profound."
World-Honored One!
The realm of the World-Honored One’s *jñeyāyatana* is difficult to fathom to its bottom.
Had I previously known that the Tathāgata’s realm was so profound and wondrous, I would rather have my body be crushed like sesame seeds than fail to reach the ultimate shore of the Buddha-dharma.
All such as these are called the practice of contemplating dependent origination.
Regarding the divisions of segments and moments: the three times are a single moment, and a single moment is the three times.
A phenomenon that has not yet arisen is called "future"; that which is arising is called "present"; and that which has already arisen is called "past.
A single moment of arising is itself a single moment, because suffering and impermanence coexist within it.

One should know that all conditioned phenomena do not abide for even a single moment; they neither come from anywhere nor go anywhere, and though they undergo transformation, they have no destination. Even as they depart, there is no accumulation.
Arising in one kṣaṇa, it ceases in one kṣaṇa;
a kṣaṇa is like a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is like a kṣaṇa.
The aggregate of the preceding kṣaṇa has already ceased, and at the time of its cessation, the subsequent [aggregate] arises.
In accordance with the fulfillment of the four conditions,
the subsequent moment arises as the sphere of cultivation.
Contemplating within a single moment, there are immeasurable atoms.
Immeasurable atoms, in each and every kṣaṇa, succeed one another in continuous succession like a string of pearls.
It is, for example, as when four skilled archers simultaneously release four arrows.
There is a man of great agility who, before an arrow has even reached the ground, can catch four arrows in mid-air so that they do not fall.

The Earth Deity is swifter than this; the Space Deity is swifter than the Earth Deity; the Sun and Moon Deities are swifter than the Space Deity; and the Vegavati Deities are twice as swift as the Sun and Moon Deities.
One should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and pass more swiftly than this, beyond the reach of analogy.

For example, when practicing contemplation, one observes that the seven-day stage of the embryo (*kalala*) contains immeasurable moments (*kṣaṇa*); one should know that all other stages are likewise so.

Having observed in this way, one leaves behind all delusion and increases clear wisdom; such immeasurable practice is called the cultivation of the observation of the momentary nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, the initial entry into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) is called the "bound-together" stage; its increase is called the "continuous flow" stage; its stabilization is called the "segmented" stage; and its gradual cessation is called the "momentary" stage.

Furthermore, having already explained the four types of specific-characteristic contemplation on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the Buddha taught the general dependent origination; this shall now be explained: the two branches of sowing, the two branches of ripening, the two branches of arising, the two branches of drawing forth, the two branches that are sown, the two branches that grow, the two branches that reach fulfillment, the two branches of experiencing, the two branches of the agent, the two branches of the field, the two branches of the depositor, and the two branches of what is deposited.
The recipient of the entrustment is said to possess the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
When practicing the contemplation of dependent origination, one contemplates either the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) or the four aggregates.
The five aggregates pertain to the desire realm and the form realm; the four aggregates pertain to the formless realm.
The various formations such as impermanence and emptiness are definitively real within the aggregates (*skandha*).

Once they are definitively real, their definitive characteristics manifest before one. Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises; because this is absent, that is absent; because this ceases, that is not produced.
It is like having a fire-drill and a fire-stick; when a person applies skillful means, smoke and fire emerge, and through the fuel, a blazing flame arises.
It is also like how there is shade because of a tree, light because of the sun, and a flame because of a lamp—all arise from conditions.
Ignorance does not say, "I can produce volitional formations";
nor do volitional formations say, "I am produced from ignorance.
One should know that all links of existence are likewise: they are empty phenomena, phenomena of cessation, and phenomena of non-existence; no agent can be found.
When ignorance and volitional formations merely come together, tainted phenomena arise.
With feeling as the axle, the wheel of the factors of existence turns, giving rise to all fetters and bonds.

Among the fetters, the factor of craving increases; among the bonds, the factor of grasping increases; among the latent tendencies, the factor of consciousness increases; and among the envelopments, ignorance increases.

The fetters of birth increase; the bonds of rebirth increase; the various consciousnesses are driven by the increase of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*); and delusion regarding objects increases through afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thus, the bonds of affliction and karma are able to produce the fruits of rebirth, causing the wheel of existence (*bhava-cakra*) to revolve perpetually.

Because ignorant sentient beings increase their attachments according to the literal meaning, it is said that there are distinctions; one should know that all factors possess fetters, underlying tendencies, and entanglements.
Furthermore, when practicing the sixfold contemplation of dependent origination, the twelve links are explained in accordance with their respective meanings.

This refers to the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) as the contemplation of the members of karma and existence; for exhalation and inhalation are bodily formations (kāyasaṃskāra), vitarka and vicāra are vocal formations (vāksaṃskāra), and perception and volition are mental formations (manaḥsaṃskāra). Therefore, mindfulness of breathing is the antidote to them.

The contemplation of the elements (*dhātu*) involves observing the factors of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and birth (*jāti*); because consciousness is predominant in entering the womb, and because consciousness is predominant among the elements, it is designated as the seven consciousness-elements. Therefore, this contemplation of the elements serves as the antidote to those [factors].

The skillful contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*) involves contemplating the factors of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); therefore, this skillful contemplation of the aggregates is the antidote to those [afflictions].

The skillful contemplation that breaks through the entry and exit of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) involves contemplating the factors of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and contact (*sparśa*); therefore, this skillful contemplation of the sense-bases is the antidote to those [afflictions].

The skillful contemplation of dependent origination involves contemplating the members of ignorance (*avidyā*) and feeling (*vedanā*); therefore, this skillful contemplation of dependent origination is their antidote. Why is that?
Feeling (*vedanā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are the roots of all afflictions; therefore, wisdom (*prajñā*) is their antidote.
Because the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) involve attachment to the pure, impurity (*aśubha*) is their antidote.

Furthermore, when practicing the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, one may proceed from cause to effect, or from effect to cause; one may proceed from ignorance and volitional formations up to old age and death; or one may contemplate from consciousness up to old age and death; or one may contemplate how the conjunction of the three factors gives rise to contact, contact gives rise to feeling, feeling gives rise to craving, craving gives rise to grasping, and so on up to old age and death; or one may proceed from craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death; or from old age and death back to ignorance; or one may contemplate from old age and death back to consciousness, as explained in the *Buddhagāra-upama-sūtra*.
Furthermore, in the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one contemplates each of the twelve links with particular emphasis:

through the foundation of mindfulness of the body, one contemplates the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); through the foundation of mindfulness of feeling, one contemplates the link of feeling (*vedanā*); through the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, one contemplates the links of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); and through the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma*), one contemplates the remaining links collectively.
Having explained this meaning, he spoke these verses of praise:
"The practice of purifying the ground through skillful means, up to the ultimate state—
the unsurpassed master of the gift of Dharma has taught this, which has been transmitted to the present day."
I have heard this from that Victorious One and compiled these profound and wondrous meanings;
this collection, adorned with verses and phrases, is intended to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time.
The Buddha-dharma is deep and bottomless; its practice is likewise boundless.
With my meager intelligence, I proclaim the immeasurable Dharma;
this profundity is beyond the reach of measurement, like a mosquito tasting the great ocean.
Only those who have already crossed over can, thereafter, reach its ultimate limit.
The sixty-two elements (*dhātu*):

the six types [of objects], the six sense faculties (*indriya*), the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), the six elements (*dhātu*), and the six perceptions (*saṃjñā*). These latter six refer to the three impure perceptions—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion—and their opposites, the three pure perceptions;
as well as the six [feelings]: suffering, pleasure, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.

Three: the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; furthermore, the dharmas of the three times within the realms of form, formlessness, and cessation; the inferior, intermediate, and superior dharmas; the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas; and the four categories of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
The second [set] consists of:

nutriment and non-nutriment; the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*); that which relies on desire and that which relies on renunciation; the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The thirty-six stages of impurity (*aśubha*) are as follows:

Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, tendons, flesh, bones, marrow, spleen, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, small intestine, large intestine, stomach, bladder, feces, urine, filth and impurities, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, pus, blood, yellow and white phlegm, snot, fat, grease, brain, and membranes.
The calculation of *kṣaṇas*:
one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*; sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*; thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*; and thirty *muhūrtas* constitute one day and night.
Within a year, there are only two occasions of two days when thirty *māhurudus* (muhūrtas) constitute an equal day and night.
These are the eighth day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) of the month of Kārttika; the eighth month is called Kārttika, and its latter half is termed the "bright fortnight."

In the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) of the month of Vaiśākha—the second month, named Vaiśākha, where the latter half of the month is called the bright fortnight—on these two days, day and night are each fifteen *muhūrtas*.

Following this, as the *lava* flows, either the day decreases while the night increases, or the night decreases while the day increases; this is called the "flowing" of day and night, each being thirty *muhūrtas*.
This refers to the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika and the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha.
The month of Kārttika refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month; this latter half of the eighth month is called the "bright fortnight.
The month of Vaiśākha refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the second month; this latter half of the second month is called the "bright fortnight."
During these two periods of two days, each day and night consists of thirty *māhuludus*.
Following this, they flow (*pravāha*); that is, either the day decreases while the night increases, or the night decreases while the day increases—this is called "flowing."
